hero.description: A cluttered backlog column of abstract ticket cards. Our ticket is red and flagged bug. As scrolling begins it lifts out of the column onto the track. Cards carry no IDs, titles, names, avatars, or PR number. The only card text is 'bug' and the Illustration tag. The hero.visualLabel sits beside the column as real text.

sixty.description: The track pauses. The ticket sits beside the summary like a ticket detail panel. The panel shows only this section's real text and the Illustration tag: no ID, key, title, assignee, reporter, sprint, priority, avatar, or other person field.

pipeline.description: One station per step. Reproduce, Fix, Verify (second agent marker with a fresh context badge), Regression, Review, Opened PR (ticket becomes a PR card). The PR card has no PR number, branch, repo, author, or avatar; before and after thumbnails are abstract shapes, never video or app images.

safety.description: The track passes a gate. A billing / auth lane stops at a human-approval checkpoint, a single retry meter fills to a cap line, and the drawn kill switch is the real control. The retry meter is one continuous bar with no discrete units, numbers, tier names, or tier count, so no cap or tier count can be read from it.

mcp.description: The track branches into tool lanes. A classifier node routes a question to one lane. A delete lane is visibly fenced off.

platform.description: The track runs through a calm grid of abstract component tiles. Small markers join the track behind the ticket to show team adoption. Markers have no initials or avatars; their count is decorative and never equals a team size stated on the site (3, 5, 9, or 35).

independent.description: Two side tracks branch off to the FoundrKids and Pocket Chronicle panels and rejoin.

career.description: The track becomes a vertical commit log. Each role is a commit with date range and title. Older commits are dimmer.

achievements.text: Sole author of an agentic engineering system at Atlas UP: 30+ Claude Code skills chained into loops that took a ticket from reproduction to a verified, opened pull request.
Used that system to clear 100+ bugs and about 25 features in about six weeks, with roughly 95% of bug tickets accepted without being bounced back.

intro.text: At Atlas UP I was the sole author of an agentic engineering system: 30+ Claude Code skills chained into loops that took a Jira ticket from reproduction to a verified, opened pull request.

visualNote.text: The ticket, track, and stations are original drawings. No real tickets, code, prompts, or screenshots appear here.

stages.label: Reproduce
stages.text: The loop started by reproducing the ticket.

stages.label: Fix
stages.text: Next, the loop made the fix.

stages.label: Verify
stages.text: A separate agent, not the one that wrote the fix, verified every fix with fresh context.

stages.label: Regression
stages.text: The change then ran through regression.

aside.label: Related: release regression
aside.text: At the release level, I built an AI regression lane that ran TestRail cases through Claude Code and Playwright, scoped by each release's blast radius. It cut a full regression cycle from about a week to 8 to 10 hours and removed QA as the release bottleneck.

aside.label: Related: PR review agent
aside.text: I also built an autonomous pull request review agent on Azure DevOps. It reviewed open PRs at their latest commit and posted severity-ranked findings, encoding team standards so I was no longer the mandatory manual review gate.

stages.label: Opened PR
stages.text: The loop ended with an opened pull request that included before and after videos.

result.text: I used the system to clear a backlog of 100+ bugs and about 25 features in about six weeks, with roughly 95% of bug tickets accepted without being bounced back.

intro.text: I was a core contributor on the team that built a production MCP server for EOS One. It let customers connect Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok to their EOS One data.

classifier.text: A question classifier routed each request to the right tool.

vue.text: I owned the Vue frontend platform for EOS One, an AI business operating system with about 10,000 monthly active users.

stack.text: The platform ran on Vue, C# and .NET, SignalR, Redis, Cosmos DB, and Python microservices.

monorepo.text: I consolidated it into a single npm monorepo and maintained a 150+ component library, which I had built from the ground up, and moved roughly 80% of it to design tokens.

library.text: Earlier, at EOS Worldwide, I built the EOS One component library from the ground up, establishing the frontend architecture, patterns, and standards the product still runs on.

shipping.text: At Atlas UP we ran a weekly release train and used Ship/Show/Ask, so changes reached production almost daily on Azure DevOps Pipelines.

review.text: At EOS Worldwide, as the sole senior engineer on a predominantly junior frontend team, I personally reviewed every frontend pull request and used review as the main lever for raising the team's baseline.

mentoring.text: After my promotion to Staff Frontend Software Engineer, Lead, I led three direct reports with one on ones and growth planning alongside hands-on delivery.

mentorship.text: I have a track record of mentoring engineers into independent contributors.

adoption.text: At Atlas UP, I led the team's AI adoption from Cursor to Claude Code to autonomous loops. The rest of the team adopted the skills after seeing the delivery rate.

standards.text: At Atlas UP, I encoded team standards into the PR review agent described in The Pipeline.

retention.text: I was retained as one of three staff engineers when the post-acquisition team went from 35 people to 9.

intro.text: I built two AI products on my own: FoundrKids, an AI maker-learning platform in pre-launch, and Pocket Chronicle, a native iOS app I shipped to the App Store and later retired.

summary.text: An AI maker-learning platform for kids 7 to 15: a chat coach guides build missions while parents track safety.

points.text: I built the full stack solo: three Vue 3 apps, a FastAPI backend with 140+ endpoints, Postgres with pgvector, Redis, and Stripe on Fly.io and Neon, plus an adaptive learning engine.

Every model call goes through a six-layer safety pipeline: blocklist, OpenAI moderation, prompt scaffolding, the model, a streaming sentence buffer, and a PII-redacting output filter. It fails closed; critical events end the session and alert the parent.
Cost-controlled model routing sends work to Anthropic or OpenAI by mission tier, with cross-vendor failover and a monthly spend cap per household.
COPPA is built into the data layer: verified parental consent, a 90-day chat purge, real child deletion, and a tamper-proof audit log.

name.note: The resume (L62) and HEADLINE_PROOF spell this with a trailing s. That is a typo; always use the singular.

status.text: Shipped to the App Store in 2026, now retired. It worked end to end but did not find users, so I shut it down rather than keep paying to run the backend.

summary.text: A family memory app I shipped solo, from concept to the App Store in about a month, by directing AI agents outside my primary stack.

points.text: Stack: SwiftUI and SwiftData with offline-first sync, StoreKit 2, Sign in with Apple, and on-device transcription and Foundation Models; FastAPI and async SQLAlchemy on Postgres, deployed to Fly.io.
Quality: about 2,700 automated tests, 200+ merged PRs, and a written spec and decision log behind every change.
